## Intent
Hypothesis: compiler auto-vectorization over per-particle AoS components can approach the streaming ceiling on death-free workloads.

## Layout & approach
The 68 B/particle AoS layout offers 128-byte cacheline fills where loop 1 touches only 32 of 68 B (47% hot — age+pos+seed+vel) and loop 2 touches 28 of 68 B (41% hot — color+pos), so over half each loop drags through the line filler is dead weight. No intermediate storage means the death verdict stays in registers, avoiding a second pass, but it also means both loops walk the full stride-68B AoS with no SoA repacking. The expected interaction with the cache hierarchy is benign: working sets spill L1d at N≈963 and L2 at N≈61680, but because only 41–47% of each cacheline is hot, the effective working set is roughly half the nominal 68·N, pushing real pressure deeper than the raw transitions suggest.

## Cache saturation
The ns/p-vs-N curve is strikingly flat. At q=0.01 it ranges 6.9–7.7 ns/p across the entire span from L1d-resident (N=380) to DRAM (N=10M), with no visible knee at the L1d→L2 transition (N≈963: 7.16→7.23) or the L2→DRAM transition (N≈62000: 7.22→7.0). The dense grid resolves no spill because the algo never approaches memory-bound operation — achieved bandwidth sits at ~32% of ceiling, so cache depth is irrelevant. Cost rises modestly through the L2-resident band (N=2400–10000, 7.47–7.72 ns/p) then settles back in DRAM, suggesting prefetch amortization rather than capacity pressure.

## Bandwidth
Achieved bandwidth peaks at 9.86 GB/s (q=0.01, N=150000) — only 33% of the 29.9 GB/s ceiling. The memory floor of 2.274 ns/p frames the algo as 3–6× above irreducible memory time, confirming it is not bandwidth-bound. At q=0.01 it is compute-bound (compute 60–70%, backend_stall 25–27%, branch_flush 4–7%). As death rate climbs the regime shifts to branch-bound: at q=0.25 branch_flush reaches 33–34% and at q=0.5 it hits 36–37%, while backend_stall collapses to 6–9%. Against baseline the algo is 0.93–0.98× naive scalar at every point — slightly slower everywhere. Against the winner it is 1.6× slower at q=0.01 (N=380: 1.927×) widening to 2.4–2.5× at q=0.5 (N=10M: 2.451×), where branch_flush dominates.

## Assembly
The codegen vectorizes minimally: 9 vector-suffixed instructions out of 295. Loop 1 uses `fmul.4s`, `fadd.4s`, `dup.4s`, and `ext.16b` to process 4-lane FP within a single particle's pos+vel, but the indexed `ld1.s` gather and scalar `fmul`/`fadd` alongside it show the compiler could not vectorize across particles. Loop 2 is entirely scalar: `csel`×18 for select-based clamping, `ldrb`/`strb`×16 for byte-granular RGBA scatter, and `fcmp`×9 for bounds checks. The branchy respawn path uses `b.ge`/`b.gt` to a `bl _layouts.ML01.data.Data.spawn` call. The byte-granular `strb` stores and scalar FP in loop 2 cap achieved bandwidth at 33% of ceiling; the 11 conditional branches per loop-1 iteration explain the branch_flush escalation with death rate.

## Verdict
Refuted — 0.96–0.98× of naive scalar at every N×q point (e.g., 0.962× at N=380, q=0.01; 0.977× at N=10M, q=0.5), meaning auto-vectorization over AoS provides no benefit over scalar, and 1.6–2.5× slower than the winner (1.927× at q=0.01, 2.451× at q=0.5). The mechanism is clear: 9/295 vector instructions cannot overcome the stride-68B AoS with 47% hot bytes, and the byte-granular `strb` scatter in loop 2 prevents streaming regardless of death rate, while branch_flush rises to 37% at q=0.5 as the branchy respawn path dominates.
